indian-startups-45591325bf.headline: DheyaTech Bags ₹43 Cr To Scale Indigenous Gas Turbine Engine Production
indian-startups-45591325bf.fulltext: Aerospace propulsion startup DheyaTech has raised ₹43 Cr (around $5.1 Mn) in a funding round led by Avaana Capital, with participation from Unimech Aerospace and Manufacturing. The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to scale production, establish an integrated testing facility for its gas turbine engines, and work with domestic and global OEMs to accelerate commercial deployments. DheyaTech is targeting flight trials of its engines in Q4 2026. The startup said it has already secured orders from Indian and global OEMs, without disclosing their names or the value of the contracts. Founded in 2018 by aerospace engineers Gurushankara KC, Abhinav Alva, and Chetan Kumar, DheyaTech develops indigenous small gas turbine engines for advanced aerial platforms and energy systems. Its engine portfolio spans thrust capacities ranging from 20 kgf to 400 kgf. The startup said the engines are now entering the commercial deployment stage after years of research and development. DheyaTech claims to have built the entire product development pipeline in-house, covering engine design, development, assembly, and testing. It has also developed a proprietary adaptive engine control unit (ECU), which manages and adjusts an engine’s operation. The startup claimed that it is the first Indian private company to pursue independent airworthiness certification for its gas turbine engines under the guidance of the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification (CEMILAC), a DRDO laboratory. Beyond propulsion, DheyaTech is expanding into hydrogen-based technologies and distributed power-generation systems. In collaboration with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bengaluru, DheyaTech has also developed a hydrogen-based flexi-fuel combustor for its 60-kW turbogenerator. A turbogenerator combines a gas turbine with an electrical generator to produce power. DheyaTech’s fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian aerospace and spacetech startups developing indigenous hardware and propulsion technologies. In January, aerospace propulsion startup D-Propulse raised ₹25 Cr from IAN Alpha Fund to develop indigenous propulsion systems based on rotating detonation engine technology. Meanwhile, spacetech startup InspeCity raised ₹100 Cr in August in a round co-led by Ashish Kacholia and Speciale Invest. It plans to use the capital to fund four in-orbit missions and advance its satellite-servicing and propulsion technologies. Advanced hardware and technology startups, including aerospace, defence, semiconductor, and robotics ventures, raised $365 Mn across 66 deals in the first half of 2026.

india-deep-tech-7dc9b869d9.headline: Indian chip startup Mindgrove Technologies eyes first revenues this fiscal year
india-deep-tech-7dc9b869d9.fulltext:
Nabodita Ganguly
Published17 Sep 2026, 06:00 AM IST
New Delhi: As India’s annual chip conference kicks off, Mindgrove Technologies, a homegrown semiconductor design startup incubated at IIT Madras, expects to start generating revenue this fiscal year, backed by "about half a dozen" clients.
In an interview with Mint, Shashwath TR, cofounder and chief executive of Mindgrove, said this will mark the first instance of the five-year-old startup earning revenue from its locally made chips integrated into industrial applications and platforms.
Generating revenue would mark a major milestone for Mindgrove, aligning with India's broader push to establish indigenous chip design as a core pillar of its nascent semiconductor ecosystem. On 31 August, S Krishnan, secretary at the ministry of electronics and IT, underlined that “building sovereign chip patents that are owned by India are crucial to the country’s interests, and the government is keen to back the semiconductor industry as required to help realize this”.
Quick answers to key questions
•5 QUESTIONS
1
What is Mindgrove Technologies and what are its plans for revenue generation?⌵
Mindgrove Technologies is an Indian semiconductor design startup aiming to generate revenue this fiscal year from its chips integrated into industrial applications, supported by approximately half a dozen clients.
2
Why is revenue generation important for Mindgrove Technologies?⌵
Generating revenue is crucial for Mindgrove as it would mark a significant milestone in its five-year journey and align with India's initiative to build a robust domestic semiconductor ecosystem.
3
How is Mindgrove Technologies planning to capture clients across various industries?⌵
Mindgrove is actively engaging in discussions and trials with potential clients across sectors like biometrics, CCTV surveillance, and metering, with several prospects nearing finalization.
4
What government support is available for semiconductor startups like Mindgrove?⌵
The Indian government offers design-linked cash incentives and funding to support domestic chip design, encouraging startups to innovate and develop proprietary chip patents.
5
Should semiconductor startups target local or international clients?⌵
Mindgrove's strategy does not differentiate between Indian and international clients, focusing instead on local demand for its chips, as the primary growth is anticipated from India's own markets.
To achieve this, Shashwath said the startup is “in active discussions and trials with customers across industries such as biometrics, CCTV surveillance, metering and other applications.” He added, “Around half a dozen prospective customers are at a stage where they could be finalised, although the timelines vary across deployments.”
Founded in February 2021, Mindgrove Technologies is building chips for use in security-first products such as connected cameras, and in robotics for artificial intelligence-related use cases.
In February 2023 it raised $2.3 million in seed funding from Peak XV Partners (then still Sequoia India) and Speciale Invest, an early-stage deep-tech venture capital fund. It followed this up with an $8-million series A funding round in December 2024, with Silicon Valley’s Rocketship VC joining its list of investors.
The company is developing two chips. The first one, designed for connected appliances such as smart cameras, will be commercially rolled out by late 2026. Shashwath confirmed that this chip “is already in use by a small number of customers, such as AtumX.”
Also Read | The race to build India’s first AI chip
AtumX, a robotics-focused education platform, is using Mindgrove’s initial commercial design to teach robotics to school students. Shashwath noted that Mindgrove’s pilot order with AtumX involves supplying an initial 500 chip-powered computing boards. “The products will be piloted in the northeast and J&K, as well as a few other places including, hopefully, Tamil Nadu. We may get a few thousand orders out of that every month.”
Companies such as Mindgrove remain far behind their Silicon Valley counterparts. For context, Nvidia acquired Groq, a Silicon Valley startup developing proprietary chips for AI chatbots, for $20 billion on 24 December 2025. Under the Semicon 2.0 incentive scheme unveiled on 15 July, the Centre has earmarked a significant portion of its ₹1.28-trillion outlay to boost domestic chip design through design-linked cash incentives (DLI) and equity funding.
Shashwath noted that Mindgrove is evaluating these government incentives and may apply. “DLI 2’s portal is not open yet. We’re in discussions with Meity to figure out what we can expect from DLI 2, and how much more we need to raise," he said.
For now, though, the company is accelerating its push to capture a larger base of paying clients, without differentiating between Indian or global ones. “I am not really differentiating between Indian and international clients at this point. Our target opportunities are all in India, and I expect the first big commercial activity in India, not internationally. That is also a reflection of the kind of chips we are making. But I’m not differentiating based on that,” he said.
Industry stakeholders, for the most part, believe this is the right approach. “For Indian chip design companies, the crux of the opportunity will lie within the ability to serve India’s own sovereign needs. For the most part, India’s chipmakers are some distance away from building products for the world. The first big growth phase will all come from local import substitution cases,” Sriram Viswanathan, founding managing partner of Silicon Valley-based venture capital firm Celesta Capital, told Mint on 5 June.

global-economics-9926842f06.headline: Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous proposition
global-economics-9926842f06.fulltext:
Anthropic’s Dario Amodei is not the first corporate CEO to suggest that excessive competition is driving the world to some socially undesirable outcome.
The safety breach disclosed by OpenAI after a swarm of its agents coordinated to breach their supposedly secure sandbox, get on the Internet and hack AI platform Hugging Face, warrants urgent action. It demonstrated the ease with which the technology can evade human control and gave concrete form to the existential fears about what it could do to humanity if not securely leashed.
The end of the world may well be nigh, as some in the AI industry have warned. These are truly scary times. But Amodei’s call for the leading artificial intelligence labs to coordinate to slow the breakneck pace of AI development, agree on safety standards and “pace the frontier”, (a call quickly endorsed by Open AI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google Deep Mind’s Demis Hassabis) is just a hi-tech version of an old proposition by corporate America – to get a pass from antitrust laws designed to protect the American economy from colluding businesses.
It is a dangerous proposition. Freeing the tech bros from antitrust constraints supposedly to allow them to get together and fix AI’s dangerous flaws, disenfranchises the everyday Americans who are most at risk from the thing, further empowering the very labs that, in their pursuit for wealth, greatness and who knows what other fantastical objectives, so casually blew past danger thresholds on many dimensions, bringing the existential threats into being.
Amodei et al’s argument, at heart, is that their businesses are trapped in a prisoner’s dilemma. If they unilaterally slow their fevered pursuit of artificial super-intelligence to make it safer, their rivals – less concerned about existential risks, of course – will get there first, with potentially devastating consequences for humankind, let alone the bottom line of the lab that took its foot off the pedal.
“Slowing down seems sensible,” said Jean Tirole, the Nobel prize-winning economist at the Toulouse School of Economics. “But that assumes coordinated slowing-down is feasible and sustainable. What happens when OpenAI, Anthropic or Grok conclude that US holdouts – or Chinese labs – are catching up? Will they resume immediately, perhaps covertly?”
As Bill Gates has written, “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it. However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead.” In this light, it might seem like a great idea for the government to encourage a friendly agreement for everybody to slow down. It is not.
The argument that excessive competition is driving a race to the bottom, is probably as old as capitalism, deployed to explain everything from environmental degradation to child labor. But it does not justify giving businesses a right to collude as they see fit. It is a call to craft government regulations to prevent businesses from competing using socially harmful tools.
Moreover, the case that excessive competition is encouraging reckless behavior is dubious. The AI labs are engaged in a winner-takes-all race, one that is extraordinarily expensive to keep going. That’s where the recklessness comes from
Amodei may be an unimpeachable guy. His call to slow the pace of AI development, bring external evaluators into the lab and increase the transparency of his operations suggests sincere concern over the risks. The drop in the price of leading tech stocks following the publication of his propositions suggests that he is willing to take a financial hit in the service of improved safety.
But the investors Amodei hopes will eagerly snap up shares in Anthropic’s IPO later this year may not be so altruistic. Tremors in capital markets suggest that raising the money to finance the trillion-dollar AI investment race is going to get tougher, discouraging strategies that might curb the leading labs’ edge over rivals. Given the incentives, granting the AI leaders a free hand to collude and self-regulate would be foolhardy.
Eric Posner, an antitrust expert at the University of Chicago Law School, said, we “shouldn’t trust companies in general about their motivations”. There is no reason to believe the AI labs, left to their own devices, would necessarily produce good, socially acceptable outcomes. Like any company, they will be calculating trade-offs, weighing risks against profits. And as Posner observed, “they don’t use the same weights as the public”.
So, how to regulate? Nothing is going to happen on this front while Trump is in office. Even after he is gone it will be tough to craft effective regulation to deal with the threats from AI without stunting innovation. There are questions about what rules to deploy, how they are enforced, and who they should apply to. And the peril of unilateral action is real. What if Beijing declines to participate? What are the risks of Chinese AI companies plowing ahead when American labs slow down? But if we could regulate nuclear power, we can probably regulate AI.
Moreover, there are viable ideas that might help even in the absence of government regulation and that don’t require stifling competition. There are proposals to tweak intellectual rights to encourage innovations that improve the safety of AI systems. Inventors of safety innovations would be rewarded by allowing them to release new AI models before their competitors. But the safety enhancements would be made immediately available to all firms.
On the stick side of the ledger, a legal liability regime could be designed to change the incentives of AI developers by punishing firms that gain from the design and deployment of an AI tool that caused harm, even if the harm was unintentional. For instance, the Hugging Face attack might have been prevented if OpenAI’s models had not been inadvertently rewarded for misbehaving during training. The fact that Amodei’s proposal does not mention legal liability suggests that AI leaders’ concern for safety does not override concern for the bottom line.
In any event, cementing in place the dominance of the frontier labs, protecting their rents and endorsing their heretofore gung-ho strategies, is not pro-safety. On the contrary, slowing down the leaders to let the laggards catch up is likely to make the AI ecosystem a safer place by inviting in desirable innovation and promoting competition along the safety dimension.
There is no fundamental conflict between safety and competition. Masters of AI who want to make this case should be viewed with skepticism.

india-71ee30fc71.headline: Does the BRICS summit signify a shift for Indian foreign policy?
india-71ee30fc71.fulltext:
With a strong pushback against unilateral western sanctions; criticism of Israel over the killing of civilians, the attacks on Lebanon, and the forced occupation of Palestinian territory; and support for UN reform as well as a BRICS payment mechanism, the New Delhi Declaration of 2026 has been likened to India’s foreign policy from its non-aligned past. But was it a compromise by New Delhi to build consensus, or will the statement, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s close engagement with the leaders of Iran, Russia, and China, have a bearing on India’s foreign policy? Ajay Bisaria and Happymon Jacob discuss the question in a conversation moderated by Suhasini Haidar.
Is the New Delhi declaration a return to non-alignment or just momentary rhetoric?
Ajay Bisaria: Broadly, the declaration is in keeping with India’s foreign policy, whether that is strategic autonomy and multi-alignment or multi-vector engagement. In terms of optics, India is more on the front foot and less apologetic than it used to be. India is getting more and more comfortable in a non-western forum, saying that it is emphatically part of it. While it doesn’t necessarily mean a shift in posture, it does suggest a greater degree of comfort with a different set of optics.
Happymon Jacob: The BRICS summit is under spotlight and things under spotlight look bigger and shinier than they really are. BRICS is a political platform; not a security platform. I don’t think India’s policy today is that of non-alignment at all. Non-alignment was a strategy for a weak state in a bipolar world. Today, we are in a different kind of world and the desire in India is to become one of the poles in a multipolar world. There is a reference to the Bandung Spirit (Non-Aligned Movement) in the BRICS declaration in pursuit of a fairer, more inclusive, and representative multilateral system. But that is nostalgia, not real policy.
How important are optics such as the Modi-Xi-Putin handshakes or the Prime Minister reaching out to the Iranian President at a time when these leaders represent the “anti-Western lobby”?
Happymon Jacob: The optics are, in some ways, the substance here. Chinese President Xi Jinping had not been to India in nearly seven years. And we had the Abu Dhabi Crown Prince (Khaled bin Zayed Al Nahyan) sitting at the same table. In some ways, the photograph is the message. At the BRICS outreach session, a lot of powers who don’t otherwise get into great power conversations were present. So, there was a lot of socialisation happening inside the platform and on its margins. But I think we should understand that this is not really having an impact on how the world is being shaped. The declaration calls for exercising restraint and protecting civilians and civilian infrastructure and pointedly recalls the respective national positions of each member. It is fantastic, but the argument here is about optics, not common positions.
Editorial | Building consensus: On the 18th BRICS Summit, the New Delhi Declaration
Ajay Bisaria: I would agree that these multilateral fora are often performative to a degree and therefore all optics matter. But in a multilateral document, you can say the silent part aloud; what a country won’t say in a national statement, it can say aloud in a high-level multilateral summit. For instance, everyone knows that the phrase “unilateral coercive measures” is about U.S. actions. So, you’re not really saying we condemn U.S. action on so-and-so date; you’re simply saying that we are against U.S. tariffs and [western] sanctions. There is an understanding now that what is said in a multilateral document can be different from a national position.
Every BRICS summit since 2022, including the 2024 summit in Russia, has made a reference to Ukraine. The New Delhi Declaration is the first time that references to Ukraine have been dropped. Why?
Ajay Bisaria: My guess would be that it was a Russian veto. In the Rio BRICS declaration last year, there was even condemnation of a Ukrainian attack on Russia without an equivalent condemnation of anything Russia had done. So this time, instead of just condemning Ukraine, they might have decided to drop the whole thing entirely. It is very disappointing that a major multilateral geopolitical forum doesn’t call for belligerents to end the war, but instead stays silent. That is an error of omission. I suspect the Russians said, no, we don’t accept it, and in the interest of having a consensus, it was dropped.
In Focus podcast | Is BRICS coming of age?
Happymon Jacob: I think India has no particular reason to push for that language to be present in the declaration because we have quite clearly sided with the Russian Federation in this war, indirectly if not directly. There must have been Russian push but I see no reason why there could not have been some neutral language to put in [references to Ukraine], given the precedent (of previous BRICS joint declarations).
The condemnation of Israel in the statement is very strong. Does this represent a shift for India given the PM’s speech on standing “shoulder to shoulder” with Israel during his visit in February 2026?
Ajay Bisaria: The big picture is that India is trying to establish neutral and balanced positions on both conflicts, and therefore not be seen as backing only one side in either. It has taken safety in the language of the United Nations. There’s a specific mention of the UN Security Council Resolution 2803 of November last year, which spoke about an International Stabilisation Force and a Board of Peace. Some of the language has been drawn from there. The overall posture is: let’s try to be balanced and reasonably neutral.
Editorial | More heft: On India and the 18th BRICS Summit
Happymon Jacob: There is a clear disjunction between the statement and what Prime Minister Modi told the Israeli parliament. Perhaps the declaration is in some way intended to counter the perception that India was getting too close to Israel. The two-state solution has always been India’s position, so the declaration doesn’t contradict Indian policy there. But with the UAE, Egypt, Iran, and Indonesia in the room, there was only so much India could do to push back against the harshness of that language. What Prime Minister Modi told the Israelis in Israel is emotional and consequential. But what is written in the BRICS Declaration is multilateral, symbolic, and not very consequential. I would still say the balance is tilted in favour of Israel as a partner.
How significant are the paragraphs on economic issues, particularly on intra-BRICS trade using payments in national currencies? These 10 or 11 countries represent 40% of the global economy, and 25% of global trade. Could they pose a challenge to the G7?
Happymon Jacob: Indian policy has two parts. One is the support for local currency payment mechanisms. I don’t think India has supported a permanent payment mechanism under the ambit of BRICS. I think there is an acknowledgement that there is no one-size-fits-all approach as far as currency settlement payment mechanisms are concerned. I would think twice before signing on to a non-U.S. dollar payment mechanism, which I believe will mean the next big currency or the next powerful currency. And unfortunately, China’s currency is going to be that big currency.
Video | BRICS gives India’s balancing power a boost
Ajay Bisaria: BRICS is a counterpoint to the G7, an economic grouping that also has geopolitical responsibilities. But I think India also finds itself at an intersection with the G7, because it is a sort of permanent invitee to the G7, along with Australia and South Korea. I have made the argument elsewhere that the G7 should dissolve itself and become the Democratic 10 (D10), including these three countries. I think that is the real strategic autonomy or multi-vector engagement, where India becomes the bridge between the east and the west, but also a voice of the south.
How much of BRICS solidarity accrues to the Trump factor, including a reaction to the latest U.S. Sanctions Bill on Russia and Iran?
Ajay Bisaria: The Trump factor is a key driver of many of these geopolitical events — if not of the substance, certainly of the optics. There is a Trump accelerator at play at BRICS, in terms of BRICS unity. It is this accelerator that gets you to get an India-EU Free Trade Agreement in record time. The Trump accelerator gets India to reverse its relationship with Canada in record time. But also, a non-western alternative grouping has a certain dynamic of its own.
Comment | A bigger BRICS, shaped by India’s vision
Happymon Jacob: Much of the threat that Mr. Trump sees in BRICS only exists in his imagination. But today, it is important to take Mr. Trump and his threats seriously. India’s primary challenge as a growing power is not the U.S.; it is China. And therefore, while we like the idea of a multipolar order, I am cognisant of the fact that if [China] becomes the most powerful country in the world, it is certainly not going to be great for India’s own national interests. Give BRICS the credit that is due to it, which is that it brings together the voice of the Global South and conveys that message to the collective west. But it is also important to note that BRICS, like several platforms, is a political platform that airs complaints and that airs unhappiness without too much geopolitical consequence on the ground.
Has India’s convening power as host been dented by the fact that there were no leaders from any of the neighbouring countries?
Happymon Jacob: India should have brought its neighbourhood together under the BRICS platform, which it had done in the past (2016 BRICS-BIMSTEC Summit). I’m not a great believer in the idea of South Asia, but I certainly believe in the instrumentality of SAARC and BIMSTEC regional organisations that can convene the countries of South Asia. China is now taking the lead not only in engaging South Asian countries bilaterally but also convening them in a group. It is a shame that the government is not able to hold on to those.
Also read | BRICS adopts New Delhi Declaration with consensus
Ajay Bisaria: It would have been a much better situation if the neighbours were present at BRICS, with the BIMSTEC countries, if not all SAARC countries, minus Pakistan and Afghanistan. But I think there were a couple of geopolitical accidents. In terms of Bangladesh, the Sheikh Hasina press conference became the trigger, and then Nepal had the floods. Even so, India’s neighbours should have been called for the ‘party’.
Will any of the decisions at BRICS see their way into future Indian foreign policy? Or is this just one moment with BRICS countries?
Ajay Bisaria: I think this is a moment of success in Indian diplomacy in terms of conducting a major international event. In November, there will be another opportunity to meet global leaders at the ASEAN-East Asia Summit in the Philippines, followed by Prime Minister Modi’s visits to the U.S., Canada, and Brussels, where he could potentially secure three trade agreements. I think that’s what diplomacy will be about: multi-vector engagement; keeping all stakeholders engaged, in multiple directions.
Comment | India’s opportunity to put BRICS back together
Happymon Jacob: India has only so much diplomatic capital. Therefore, it is important to pick our battles, forums, and partners. I think we should be present in those rooms where global rules on AI are being framed, and where the future of space governance is discussed. I don’t think the next world order is going to be made in forums such as the BRICS but in those silent small rooms.

The introduction of the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) will help more domestic payments companies to operate under UPI, contrary to the allegation that the charge has been introduced under external pressure, the government said on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
The public sector National Payments Council of India (NPCI) on Wednesday announced the MDR structure on UPI payments prompting criticism from the Opposition and allegations that U.S. pressure had pushed the Indian government to introduce this charge.
“Contrary to misleading claims made that MDR has been introduced under external pressure, introduction of MDR on select high-value transactions will enable more domestic companies to operate under UPI,” the Department of Financial Services (DFS) said on X. “Thus, the action of introduction of MDR is a step in protecting India’s sovereignty in the electronic payment ecosystem.”
The DFS further said that the allegations of U.S. pressure refer to a report by the U.S. Trade Representative in which it cites the inability of American electronic payment services suppliers to participate in the UPI ecosystem, including credit transactions on UPI, on a level playing field with RuPay.
The DFS said that the actions by the NPCI do not rectify these American concerns.
“The NPCI circular of 15.9.2026 does not allow credit transactions of UPI by any other credit card other than RuPay credit card,” the DFS clarified. ‘There is a clear policy of only allowing RuPay credit card on UPI to enable RuPay credit card to become the preferred choice of credit card amongst users in India.”
The USTR report also raised the issue of an NPCI rule mandating a maximum market share of 30% for third-party apps as a potential hindrance. Here, too, the DFS said that while the rule was put in place, enforcement was not possible due to market conditions.
“Although NPCI had mandated market share limitation of 30% for third-party application providers in November 2020, however, this mandate could not be implemented because companies other than the market leaders could not compete in absence of a self-sustaining revenue model,” the DFS said.
A previous analysis by The Hindu shows that India’s UPI market is dominated by American companies, with Walmart-owned PhonePe holding a market share of about 46% and Google Pay with 32% in the total volume of UPI transactions conducted in the country.
“Introduction of MDR on select high-value transactions will provide a self-sustaining revenue model to smaller companies to compete for higher share in the UPI ecosystem,” the DFS said. “Thus, introduction of MDR has been done with the intention of allowing more domestic companies to expand their operations.”

Abhishek Sharma hits 30-ball century, breaks Rohit Sharma's Indian record in T20Is
Abhishek Sharma broke a series of records with a blistering 30-ball century during India's third T20I against Afghanistan in New Delhi on Thursday. He became the first batter in history to hit two centuries in less than 40 deliveries in T20Is.
Abhishek Sharma smashed the fastest T20I century by an Indian, bringing up his third hundred in the format in just 30 balls in the series finale against Afghanistan at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Thursday. He broke Rohit Sharma’s record for the fastest T20I century by an Indian, with the former captain having previously reached his hundred in 35 deliveries against Sri Lanka in 2017.
Abhishek had smashed 10 sixes and nine boundaries by the time he reached his hundred, with the team total reading 132 for 0 in 8.3 overs. The Afghanistan bowlers let down their captain after Ibrahim Zadran won the toss and opted to field.
After reaching his hundred, Abhishek sat on the pitch and struck a meditation pose, mimicking the celebration made famous by Manchester City striker Erling Haaland.
Abhishek was looking set for a daddy hundred, with plenty of time to double his score, but he was dismissed by Rashid Khan for 108 (34 balls) in the 10th over.
Nonetheless, Abhishek Sharma became the first batter in the history of T20 internationals to hit two centuries in less than 40 deliveries. Earlier, he had smashed a 37-ball hundred against England at Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai in 2025. It was also his third century in the shortest format of the game.
Varun Chakravarthy had said after the first T20I in Delhi: “Against our batting line-up, you can’t bowl spin.”
Afghanistan could neither bowl spin nor pace as the Indian batters feasted on their bowling throughout the ‘Friendship Cup’, which was anything but friendly on the field. On Thursday, Abhishek ensured his teammate’s words rang in the heads of the Afghan bowlers.
ABHISHEK’S CENTURY IN NUMBERS
- 30: Abhishek now holds the record for the fastest hundred by a batter against a Test-playing nation.
- 1: He has the fastest hundred by an Indian in T20I cricket.
- 2: Abhishek Sharma is the only batter in T20I history to score two hundred in less than 30 deliveries.
- 3: It’s the third-fastest hundred in T20I history after Sahil Chauhan's 27-ball hundred for Estonia against Cyprus in 2024 and Muhammad Fahad's 29-ball hundred for Turkey against Bulgaria in 2025.
- 4: Abhishek also became only the fourth Indian batter to score three or more hundreds in men’s T20Is.
Abhishek Sharma has wonderfully lapped up the opportunities that have come his way in the ongoing T20I series against Afghanistan. There was pressure on him, considering he was competing with 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Sanju Samson for the openers’ spots. Before the series in Delhi, Abhishek had been on a lean run, going without a fifty in seven innings — a stretch that included four single-digit scores.
76 OFF 22 IN POWERPLAY
However, Abhishek made his mark as early as the series opener, smashing a 32-ball 82 in India’s one-sided win on Sunday. He followed it up with a blistering 39 in the second T20I.
And his fireworks hit a crescendo on Thursday. With India batting first for the first time in the series, Abhishek made his intentions clear as early as the first over, lofting Fazalhaq Farooqi for a lovely drive through the covers.
He did not spare Azmatullah Omarzai in the second over either, dancing down the track against the medium-pacer and finding the boundaries, flaunting his form and confidence. The third over was a bloodbath as Farooqi was taken down by the left-hander, who collected 23 runs from the over.
Sanju Samson was a mere spectator in the first three overs as Abhishek enjoyed the pace early in his innings.
Samson took down the spinners, Mujeeb Ur Rahman and Mohammad Nabi, in the powerplay. Abhishek did not take long to join the party as the double-engine attack came together in the fifth over, which cost Afghanistan 29 runs.
Abhishek did not even hold back against Rashid Khan, who was bowling in the powerplay for the first time in the series. The left-hander was in the zone, hitting two boundaries through the covers before lofting one over long-on and into the stands.
Abhishek showed some respect to Abdullah Ahmadzai, a fresh face in the Afghanistan bowling unit, when the right-hander bowled two boundaries. But in the very next over, Abhishek had the opportunity to free his arms against Mujeeb before reaching his hundred in the ninth over.
Abhishek’s improved ability to play all around the ground will be a headache for opposition bowlers. He was suspect against off-spin earlier this year — a weakness that opposition teams looked to exploit in the T20 World Cup. However, by taking down Rashid and Co., Abhishek has sent a clear message to his detractors and analysts in the opposition camp.
At 26, Abhishek is already proving to be one of India’s finest T20I openers. Rohit Sharma’s record tally of five hundreds is the next milestone in sight. If his form in Delhi is anything to go by, he might go for it when India begin their Asian Games campaign in Japan later this month.

AIIS Research Fellowships 2026–27: Applications Open for Scholars Conducting Research on India
The American Institute of Indian Studies (AIIS) has opened applications for its 2026–27 Research Fellowship Competition, offering scholars an opportunity to undertake research connected to India. The programme provides three fellowship pathways: the Junior Research Fellowship, AIIS NEH Senior Research Fellowship, and Early Career Scholar Travel Fellowship.
The application deadline for the 2026 AIIS Fellowship Competition is November 19, 2026. Applicants are encouraged to carefully review the requirements for their selected fellowship, as each category has distinct eligibility criteria and application instructions.
Fellowship Opportunities
The Junior Research Fellowship is designed for doctoral students conducting research in Indian Studies. Non-US citizens may apply provided they are enrolled as doctoral students at a US institution.
The AIIS NEH Senior Research Fellowship supports established scholars pursuing advanced research related to India, while the Early Career Scholar Travel Fellowship provides travel support for eligible early-career researchers.
Applicants who are not affiliated with an AIIS member institution are also welcome to apply.
Junior Fellowship Application Requirements
Junior Fellowship applicants must submit a comprehensive application containing biographical and scholarly information, the proposed project title and discipline, a 350-word project abstract, and a 150-word fieldwork justification statement.
The application must also include a short CV of no more than two pages and unofficial transcripts from undergraduate and graduate institutions.
Applicants are required to submit a project statement of no more than 2,100 words explaining the proposed research. The statement should clearly present the research questions and rationale, explain the project’s significance and relationship to existing scholarship, outline the research methodology, and provide a timetable for completing the project. The word count must be included at the end of the statement.
A 1–3 page bibliography must demonstrate how the proposed research engages with relevant existing scholarship.
Applicants must also provide a personal statement of no more than 350 words, offering additional context that is not addressed elsewhere in the application. This may include relevant experiences, inspiration, challenges, or biographical information.
Applicants who previously applied unsuccessfully for an AIIS Junior Fellowship with the same project may optionally submit a revision statement of up to 500 words, explaining how the new application has been improved.
A financial aid statement is also required.
How Applications Are Evaluated
AIIS evaluates applications through a rigorous two-round review process. In the first round, reviewers assess information submitted through the application form, including the CV, project abstract, and fieldwork justification.
Finalists proceed to the second round, where reviewers assess the project statement, bibliography, personal statement, and revision statement where applicable.
The selection committee considers four major factors: the excellence and merit of the project, project design and methodology, the candidate’s academic or professional record, and financial need.
Because reviewers come from different disciplines within Indian Studies, applicants are strongly encouraged to explain their research in clear language that can be understood by scholars outside their specific field. Excessive jargon should be avoided.
Important Fellowship Conditions
All AIIS Fellows, regardless of citizenship, must obtain a Certificate of Affiliation with an Indian research centre. US citizens must obtain either a research visa or, where applicable, special research permission for OCI cardholders. AIIS assists Fellows in obtaining the necessary documentation for research in India.
Fellowship recipients must provide proof of travel before receiving their award. Travel must generally take place within two years of selection.
AIIS has limited fellowship funding. Applicants who receive another research fellowship or scholarship exceeding $10,000 cannot hold both awards simultaneously and may be required to relinquish the AIIS fellowship so that the funding can be awarded to another scholar.
Incomplete applications will not be considered.
Mentoring and Application Support
AIIS offers a mentoring service for Junior Fellowship applicants who do not have faculty advisers with South Asia expertise at their home institutions. This service can provide valuable guidance to applicants developing their research proposals.
AIIS will also host a successful application webinar on October 9, 2026, designed to provide practical guidance on preparing a competitive fellowship application. Applicants can also review webinars from previous years and examine examples of successful Junior Fellowship project statements.
Application Deadline and Submission
The application deadline for the 2026 AIIS Fellowship Competition is November 19, 2026. Prospective applicants should begin preparing their research statements, supporting documents, transcripts, bibliography, and financial information well before the deadline.
Junior Fellowship applicants can access the application through the official AIIS application portal. Finalists are expected to be announced by mid-March, with fellowship recipients announced by early May.
The AIIS Research Fellowship Competition represents a significant opportunity for scholars seeking to deepen research on India while developing rigorous, field-based scholarship. Applicants with strong research proposals, clearly defined methodologies, relevant academic or professional records, and demonstrated financial need are encouraged to prepare carefully and submit complete applications before the deadline.

The ECOWAS National Biometric Identity Card (ENBIC) has so far been deployed by seven member states: Nigeria, Ghana, Benin, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, The Gambia and Sierra Leone. The regional bloc has committed to working towards mutual acceptance of the card at air, land and sea borders by December 2026.
The biometric card is designed to replace the handwritten ECOWAS Travel Certificate with a harmonised and machine-readable travel document that allows immigration authorities to authenticate travellers electronically.
Speaking at an ENBIC media sensitisation workshop in Lagos, Head of Border Management and Migration at the ECOWAS Commission, Obinna Ajugwo, said the initiative was developed to address identity-management and cross-border movement challenges as mobility within the region increases.

The ENBIC contains a biometric chip carrying the holder’s identity information. At border points, immigration officials can use the card’s digital features to authenticate the document and verify the identity of the person presenting it. The system is also intended to improve information sharing and verification among immigration authorities in participating member states.
For Nigeria, the Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS) will remain responsible for balancing smoother movement of legitimate travellers with effective border controls. Nigeria officially began its ENBIC rollout in November 2025, following a launch by the Federal Government through the NIS.

The introduction of ENBIC, however, does not eliminate immigration checks. Border officials will still need to authenticate the card, verify that the traveller is its legitimate holder and determine the person’s admissibility in line with applicable immigration requirements.
The card’s security architecture includes digital authentication features designed to detect alterations to information stored on the biometric chip. This is expected to strengthen identity assurance while reducing reliance on paper-based verification.

He said the success of ENBIC should not be measured only by the number of cards issued, but also by whether it improves the experience of people whose livelihoods depend on cross-border movement, including traders, young people and border communities.
“By enhancing identity assurance and facilitating the movement of legitimate migrants, ENBIC contributes to a more efficient, secure and integrated mobility framework,” Ibrahim said.

Travellers seeking to remain beyond the permitted period are required to comply with the residence requirements of the host country.
